abstract: Light is a powerful tool to study animal behavior.1-3 In contrast to natural light, almost all artificial light exhibits flicker, but most work on insect behavioral responses to light flicker focuses on flicker perceptual detection. We tested photopreference light-choice behavior across a wide range of Drosophila species in response to rhythmically flickering light using custom FLASH (flickering light of actuatable spectral hues) instrumentation and find species-specific behavioral responses and altered time-of-day-ordered behaviors that are evoked by light frequencies far beyond perceptual flicker frequency. Mutant analysis shows that behavioral responses to FLASH rely on all known classes of phototransduction, including Cryptochrome and Rhodopsin-7 expressed directly in brain neurons and the eyes. FLASH behavioral responses are abolished following ablation of the pigment-dispersing factor (PDF)-positive lateral ventral neuron circadian light input hub and in circadian mutants. These results suggest means for designing ecologically friendly light devices for species-specific insect behavioral control.
